claim: Stargazin (γ2) was identified as the prototype transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory protein (TARP).
source: Since the identification of the protein Stargazin, also known as γ2, as the prototype transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory protein (TARP) (Chen et al., 2000), several families of auxiliary proteins for the AMPA receptor have been described that include TARPs (Schwenk et al., 2012; Tomita et al., 2003), cornichons (Schwenk et al., 2009), GSG1L (Shanks et al., 2012) and CKAMPs (von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2000, which is the original work identifying Stargazin/γ2 as a TARP.

claim: Several families of auxiliary proteins for the AMPA receptor have been described including TARPs, cornichons, GSG1L, and CKAMPs.
source: Since the identification of the protein Stargazin, also known as γ2, as the prototype transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory protein (TARP) (Chen et al., 2000), several families of auxiliary proteins for the AMPA receptor have been described that include TARPs (Schwenk et al., 2012; Tomita et al., 2003), cornichons (Schwenk et al., 2009), GSG1L (Shanks et al., 2012) and CKAMPs (von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work describing these auxiliary protein families.

claim: Auxiliary proteins play an essential role in tethering AMPA-type glutamate receptors at the synapse.
source: These proteins play an essential role in tethering AMPA-type glutamate receptors at the synapse, and also exert complex control over surface expression of functional receptors (Dakoji et al., 2003; Yamazaki et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dakoji et al., 2003 and Yamazaki et al., 2010.

claim: Auxiliary proteins exert complex control over surface expression of functional AMPA receptors.
source: These proteins play an essential role in tethering AMPA-type glutamate receptors at the synapse, and also exert complex control over surface expression of functional receptors (Dakoji et al., 2003; Yamazaki et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dakoji et al., 2003 and Yamazaki et al., 2010.

claim: Auxiliary proteins regulate the function of AMPA receptors with both positive and negative modulation of gating.
source: Auxiliary proteins regulate the function of AMPA receptors, with both positive and negative modulation of gating (von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Priel et al., 2005; McGee et al., 2015; Rouach et al., 2005), as well as control over permeation and block (Soto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work on AMPAR modulation.

claim: Auxiliary proteins control permeation and block of AMPA receptors.
source: Auxiliary proteins regulate the function of AMPA receptors, with both positive and negative modulation of gating (von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Priel et al., 2005; McGee et al., 2015; Rouach et al., 2005), as well as control over permeation and block (Soto et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Soto et al., 2007.

claim: Auxiliary subunits show striking regional and cell-type specific expression.
source: The range of auxiliary subunit influence over synaptic transmission is compounded by striking regional and cell-type specific expression (Tomita et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2007), and a patchwork of interaction patterns (Bats et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2003 and Kato et al., 2007.

claim: TARPs and other auxiliary proteins modify the gating and pharmacology of synaptic AMPA receptors.
source: TARPs and other auxiliary proteins modify the gating and pharmacology of synaptic AMPA receptors (Boudkkazi et al., 2014; Milstein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boudkkazi et al., 2014 and Milstein et al., 2007.

claim: The physiological importance of modulation is likely to be the specialization of particular codes of short-term plasticity in the hippocampus and cerebellum.
source: The physiological importance of modulation is likely to be the specialization of particular codes of short-term plasticity, in the hippocampus and cerebellum at least (von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Klaassen et al., 2016; Khodosevich et al., 2014; Devi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work on short-term plasticity.

claim: Antagonists of AMPA receptors that target GluA2–γ8 complexes were recently described.
source: Recently, antagonists of AMPA receptors that target GluA2–γ8 complexes were described (Maher et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2016), further enhancing interest in the molecular basis of complexes of GluA subunits and their auxiliary proteins as potential drug targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maher et al., 2016 and Kato et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies showed that some of the effects of auxiliary proteins on receptor gating were due to the extracellular domains.
source: Previous studies showed that some of the effects of auxiliary proteins on receptor gating were due to the extracellular domains (Tomita et al., 2005; Tomita et al., 2007; Cho et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tomita et al., 2005, Tomita et al., 2007, and Cho et al., 2007.

claim: γ5 was subsequently shown to modulate gating and conductance of GluA receptors.
source: However, several of these studies made use of chimeras with γ5, which was presumed to be a null subunit, but which was subsequently shown to modulate gating and conductance of GluA receptors (Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Soto et al., 2009.

claim: Some mutations in extracellular portions of TARPs were reported that affect TARP activity, but there is no clear indication that these TARPs formed complexes with GluA subunits.
source: Although some mutations in extracellular portions of TARPs were reported that affect TARP activity, there is no clear indication that these TARPs formed complexes with GluA subunits as well (Cais et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cais et al., 2014.

claim: Different TARP isoforms show variable stoichiometry of assembly.
source: Given the variable stoichiometry of assembly between different TARP isoforms (Kim et al., 2010; Hastie et al., 2013), interpreting these data, which combine the strength of association, expression and modulation into a single metric, is difficult.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Hastie et al., 2013.

claim: A recent chimeric approach confirmed that transmembrane interactions are important for proper assembly, with the TM3 and TM4 segments of γ2 and the M1-M3 helices of the AMPA receptor determining complex assembly.
source: Very recently, a chimeric approach confirmed impressions from structural studies that transmembrane interactions are important for proper assembly, with the TM3 and TM4 segments of γ2 and the M1-M3 helices of the AMPA receptor determining complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ben-Yaacov et al., 2017.

claim: The C-termini of both the AMPA receptor and TARPs appear to be involved in complex assembly.
source: However, the C-termini of both the AMPA receptor and TARPs also appear to be involved (Ben-Yaacov et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ben-Yaacov et al., 2017.

claim: There is very little information about the extent to which different domains contribute to gating of complexes.
source: Despite these insights, there is very little information about the extent to which different domains contribute to gating of complexes (Twomey et al., 2017a), and no information about the structural basis of slow modulation, superactivation (Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Twomey et al., 2017a.

claim: There is no information about the structural basis of slow modulation, superactivation.
source: Despite these insights, there is very little information about the extent to which different domains contribute to gating of complexes (Twomey et al., 2017a), and no information about the structural basis of slow modulation, superactivation (Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carbone and Plested, 2016.

claim: γ2 and γ8 are two of the predominant TARPs in the brain.
source: Two of the predominant TARPs in the brain are the auxiliary proteins γ2 and γ8.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The extracellular segments of γ2 and γ8 are responsible for modulation of gating.
source: In this work, we isolate the extracellular segments of γ2 and γ8 that are responsible for modulation of gating, and show that these segments act on the receptor via the linkers connecting the ligand binding domain (LBD) and the transmembrane domain (TMD).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The extracellular segments of γ2 and γ8 act on the receptor via the linkers connecting the ligand binding domain (LBD) and the transmembrane domain (TMD).
source: In this work, we isolate the extracellular segments of γ2 and γ8 that are responsible for modulation of gating, and show that these segments act on the receptor via the linkers connecting the ligand binding domain (LBD) and the transmembrane domain (TMD).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: 'Null' TARPs can be produced that assemble normally but show no modulation of gating.
source: In so doing, we were able to produce 'null' TARPs, which assemble normally but show no modulation of gating.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Crystal structures of Claudins enabled a more refined view of TARP structure, defining a folded extracellular 'cap'.
source: Crystal structures of Claudins, proteins with close homology to TARPs, enabled a more refined view, defining a folded extracellular 'cap' (Suzuki et al., 2014; Saitoh et al., 2015; Shinoda et al., 2016) that substantially limits the sections of the extracellular portion of TARPs that are able to interact with the AMPA receptor, and therefore the likely range of these interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2014, Saitoh et al., 2015, and Shinoda et al., 2016.

claim: Cryo-EM/single particle analysis of GluA2-TARP complexes allowed unambiguous positioning of TARPs at the periphery of the GluA2 pore.
source: More recently, cryo-EM/single particle analysis of GluA2-TARP complexes allowed unambiguous positioning of TARPs at the periphery of the GluA2 pore, and partially resolved the extracellular domains of TARPs (Twomey et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Twomey et al., 2016 and Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: The major sequence and structural differences between TARPs with different modulatory effects are found in the variable extracellular loops between β1 and β2 (Loop 1), and between TM3 and β5 (Loop 2).
source: The major sequence and structural differences between Claudin and TARP proteins, and between TARPs with different modulatory effects, are found in the variable extracellular loops between β1 and β2 (Loop 1), and between TM3 and β5 (Loop 2, Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the topology of TARPs.

claim: Structural models of TARP γ2 and γ8 were generated based on the crystal structure of claudin15.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the related claudin15 (PDB code: 4P79) we first generated structural models of TARP γ2 and γ8 including the presumably flexible loop 1, which is not resolved in the cryo-EM AMPA-γ2 complex structures (PDB code: 5KBU and 5KK2).
evidence: The claim describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Loop 1 is not resolved in the cryo-EM AMPA-γ2 complex structures.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the related claudin15 (PDB code: 4P79) we first generated structural models of TARP γ2 and γ8 including the presumably flexible loop 1, which is not resolved in the cryo-EM AMPA-γ2 complex structures (PDB code: 5KBU and 5KK2).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of published cryo-EM structures.

claim: The in silico models of γ2 and γ8 revealed bad bonds and angles of 0.3% and 1.4% for γ2 and 0.2% and 1.6% for γ8.
source: The analysis of the in silico models revealed bad bonds and angles of 0.3% and 1.4% for γ2 and 0.2% and 1.6% for γ8.
evidence: The claim is based on MolProbity analysis of the structural models.

claim: TARP loop 2 (L2) could engage in the receptor's pore four-fold symmetry.
source: Whereas TARP loop 2 (L2) could engage in the receptor's pore four-fold symmetry, loop 1 (L1) reaches up to the two-fold symmetry of the LBD layer.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from the models.

claim: Loop 1 (L1) reaches up to the two-fold symmetry of the LBD layer.
source: Whereas TARP loop 2 (L2) could engage in the receptor's pore four-fold symmetry, loop 1 (L1) reaches up to the two-fold symmetry of the LBD layer.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from the models.

claim: L2 can interact four times in the same way with the receptor.
source: In other words, while L2 can interact four times in the same way with the receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), L1 has at least two distinct modes of interaction depending on to which receptor subunits the TARP is adjacent (subunit A-D and B-C, Figure 1B, or A-B and C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from the models, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: L1 has at least two distinct modes of interaction depending on to which receptor subunits the TARP is adjacent.
source: In other words, while L2 can interact four times in the same way with the receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), L1 has at least two distinct modes of interaction depending on to which receptor subunits the TARP is adjacent (subunit A-D and B-C, Figure 1B, or A-B and C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from the models, with reference to figures.

claim: The variable loop 1 is not resolved in structures to date, consistent with it being a flexible modulatory element.
source: The variable loop 1 is not resolved in structures to date, consistent with it being a flexible modulatory element.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of published structures and inference about the functional implications.

claim: Superactivation of GluA2 receptors resembles strongly the slow modulation of AMPA receptors by particular allosteric modulators that bind at the dimer interface.
source: Superactivation of GluA2 receptors resembles strongly the slow modulation of AMPA receptors by particular allosteric modulators that bind at the dimer interface (Kato et al., 2010; Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kato et al., 2010 and Carbone and Plested, 2016.

claim: Repeated peptide mapping array assays indicated no clear preference for either monomeric or dimeric GluA2 LBD.
source: Repeated peptide mapping array assays indicated no clear preference for either monomeric or dimeric GluA2 LBD.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide mapping arrays.

claim: The majority of the L1 of both γ2 and γ8 contain hits in the peptide mapping array, indicating direct interaction with the receptor LBD.
source: However, in accordance with our hypothesis the majority of the L1 of both γ2 and γ8 contain hits (dark spots within the purple boxes, Figure 1C) in the peptide mapping array, indicating direct interaction with the receptor LBD (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), albeit in conditions lacking the usual steric constraints of the complex.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide mapping arrays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A possible interaction between a conserved negatively charged region (negative patch) located on the TARP β4-TM2 loop and the KGK motif in the lower lobe of the GluA2 LBD was predicted in recent cryo-EM structures.
source: In the recent cryo-EM structures of the GluA2-TARP complex a possible interaction between a conserved negatively charged region (negative patch, NP) located on the TARP β4-TM2 loop and the KGK motif in the lower lobe of the GluA2 LBD was predicted (Zhao et al., 2016; Twomey et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2016 and Twomey et al., 2016.

claim: No hits were found for the negative patch in the peptide mapping array.
source: Thus we also tested for this potential interaction in the peptide mapping array but found no hits.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide mapping arrays.

claim: Neutralizing three of the six acidic residues in the negative patch (D88G, E90S, D92G) made γ2 into a much stronger modulator of AMPAR gating, with the steady-state current and superactivation both doubled.
source: A functional test of neutralizing three of the six acidic residues in this patch (D88G, E90S, D92G) made γ2 into a much stronger modulator of AMPAR gating, with the steady-state current and superactivation both doubled (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: If interactions of the TARP negative patch with the receptor alter function, they actually inhibit the action of γ2.
source: This result suggested that if interactions of the TARP negative patch with the receptor alter function, they actually inhibit the action of γ2.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that neutralizing the negative patch enhances modulation.

claim: No interaction was found between L2 peptides and the GluA2 LBD in the peptide mapping array.
source: Considering L2 being positioned distant underneath the LBD (around 15 Å, measured between Cα of GluA2 Pro717 and γ2 Lys170 in the complex from PDB code: 5KBU [Twomey et al., 2016]) in the cryo-EM structures, it was not surprising that we found no interaction between L2 peptides and the GluA2 LBD.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide mapping arrays and structural analysis.

claim: In both γ2 and γ8, L2 is adjacent to the receptor S1-M1 and S2-M4 linkers.
source: According to our GluA2-TARP models, in both γ2 and γ8, L2 is adjacent to the receptor S1-M1 and S2-M4 linkers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), which are outside the realms of our LBD construct.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: γ2 and γ8 apparently affect AMPA receptor desensitization similarly, but γ8 slows down entry to desensitization more than γ2 (60 ± 5 s–1 and 40 ± 5 s–1, n = 24 and 9, for γ2 and γ8, respectively).
source: Although γ2 and γ8 apparently affect AMPA receptor desensitization similarly, γ8 slows down entry to desensitization more than γ2 (60 ± 5 s–1 and 40 ± 5 s–1, n = 24 and 9, for γ2 and γ8, respectively; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Table 1.

claim: The chimera of γ2 with L1 from γ8 had steady-state current of 50 ± 5% (n = 30), twice as large as γ2 alone (25 ± 2%, n = 24 patches).
source: When activated by 10 mM glutamate, the chimera of γ2 with L1 from γ8 had steady-state current of 50 ± 5% (n = 30; Figure 2A and D and Table 1), twice as large as γ2 alone (25 ± 2%, n = 24 patches), and the rate of entry to desensitization was approximately halved (35 ± 5 s−1, n = 30; Figure 2C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The chimera of γ2 with L1 from γ8 had a rate of entry to desensitization approximately halved (35 ± 5 s−1, n = 30) compared to γ2 alone.
source: When activated by 10 mM glutamate, the chimera of γ2 with L1 from γ8 had steady-state current of 50 ± 5% (n = 30; Figure 2A and D and Table 1), twice as large as γ2 alone (25 ± 2%, n = 24 patches), and the rate of entry to desensitization was approximately halved (35 ± 5 s−1, n = 30; Figure 2C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The γ8 chimera with L1 from γ2 maintained the original desensitization behavior of the parent TARP (45 ± 1 s–1, n = 28).
source: In contrast, the γ8 chimera with L1 from γ2 maintained the original desensitization behavior of the parent TARP (45 ± 1 s–1, n = 28; Figure 2A and C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Deletion of L1 from γ2 and γ8 approximately halved the steady state current (15 ± 2 and 15 ± 3%, n = 11 and 15, for γ2 ΔL1 and γ8 ΔL1, respectively).
source: Deletion of L1 from γ2 and γ8 approximately halved the steady state current (15 ± 2 and 15 ± 3%, n = 11 and 15, for γ2 ΔL1 and γ8 ΔL1, respectively; Figure 2B and D and Table 1), with a barely detectable speeding up of entry to desensitization (60 ± 5 s–1, n = 11 and 15, for γ2 ΔL1 and γ8 ΔL1, respectively; Figure 2B and C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: L1 can influence desensitization of complexes.
source: These results suggested that L1 can influence desensitization of complexes, as shown recently for GSG1L (Twomey et al., 2017a) but the absence of a simple exchange in desensitization behavior suggested that this loop functions in concert with other modulatory elements.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and inference, with a citation to Twomey et al., 2017a for comparison.

claim: L1 functions in concert with other modulatory elements.
source: These results suggested that L1 can influence desensitization of complexes, as shown recently for GSG1L (Twomey et al., 2017a) but the absence of a simple exchange in desensitization behavior suggested that this loop functions in concert with other modulatory elements.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing asymmetric effects of L1 swaps.

claim: Replacement of L2 with a flexible Gly-Ser linker had a striking effect on γ2, reducing the steady state current to the level of receptors without any TARP present (5 ± 1% and 5 ± 1%, n = 15 and 9 for A2 + γ2 L2_GS and A2 WT, respectively).
source: Replacement of the L2 segment with a flexible Gly-Ser linker, predicted to be of sufficient length not to disrupt the overall structure of the extracellular domain, had a striking effect on γ2. The rate of entry to desensitization was still slower than in receptors formed of GluA2 wild type (WT) alone (65 ± 5 s−1 and 120 ± 15 s−1, n = 15 and 9 patches for A2 + γ2 L2_GS and A2 WT, respectively; Figure 3A and C and Table 1), but the steady state current was reduced to the level of receptors without any TARP present (5 ± 1% and 5 ± 1%, n = 15 and 9 for A2 + γ2 L2_GS and A2 WT, respectively; Figure 3A and D and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: There was no detectable effect on γ8 of mutating L2, except for a further slowing down of the desensitization rate (kdes = 25 ± 5 s−1, Iss = 40 ± 4%, n = 6, for γ8 L2_GS).
source: In contrast, there was no detectable effect on γ8 of mutating this loop, except for a further slowing down of the desensitization rate (kdes = 25 ± 5 s−1, Iss = 40 ± 4%, n = 6, for γ8 L2_GS; Figure 3A,C and D and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: A chimera of γ2 with the GS-linker replacing L2, but harboring the long L1 loop of γ8, massively slowed entry to desensitization, producing complexes about 10-fold slower than receptors without any TARP (kdes = 10 ± 0.5 s–1, n = 7).
source: Even more striking were results of coexpression of a chimera of γ2 with the GS-linker replacing L2, but harboring the long L1 loop of γ8. This chimera massively slowed entry to desensitization, producing complexes about 10-fold slower than receptors without any TARP (kdes = 10 ± 0.5 s–1, n = 7; Figure 3B and C and Table 1), and increased the steady state current during a 500 ms pulse of glutamate (45 ± 3%, n = 7; Figure 3B and D and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Making the inverse chimera (L1 from γ2 in γ8, with the GS-linker replacing L2) effectively nullified the modulatory activity of γ8.
source: Making the inverse chimera (L1 from γ2 in γ8, with the GS-linker replacing L2) effectively nullified the modulatory activity of γ8.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings.

claim: All mutants gave responses that were strongly reduced in rectification, indicating that complex formation between mutant TARPs and AMPAR subunits was normal.
source: Importantly, all mutants gave responses that were strongly reduced in rectification, indicating that complex formation between mutant TARPs and AMPAR subunits was normal.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from G-V measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each chimera closely followed the polyamine relief induced by the parent TARP, with γ2 chimeras producing populations of receptors that exhibited a greater rectification index than those based on γ8.
source: Broadly, each chimera closely followed the polyamine relief induced by the parent TARP, with γ2 chimeras producing populations of receptors that exhibited a greater rectification index than those based on γ8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from G-V measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: γ8 is a much stronger modifier of superactivation than γ2.
source: TARPs induce a subtype-specific superactivation of the GluA2 homomeric receptor. γ8 is a much stronger modifier of this slow gating mode than γ2 (Kato et al., 2010; Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kato et al., 2010 and Carbone and Plested, 2016.

claim: Loop 1 from γ8 could transfer the same degree of superactivation to γ2 (L1 γ8 in γ2, 27 ± 6%, n = 10).
source: In the chimeras swapping loop 1 between γ8 and γ2, the results were asymmetric (Figure 4). That is, loop 1 from γ8 could transfer the same degree of superactivation to γ2 (L1 γ8 in γ2, 27 ± 6%, n = 10; Figure 4A and C and Table 1) but the reverse swap could not reduce superactivation to the level of γ2 (L1 γ2 in γ8, 16 ± 1%, n = 16; Figure 4B and C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The reverse swap (L1 γ2 in γ8) could not reduce superactivation to the level of γ2 (L1 γ2 in γ8, 16 ± 1%, n = 16).
source: In the chimeras swapping loop 1 between γ8 and γ2, the results were asymmetric (Figure 4). That is, loop 1 from γ8 could transfer the same degree of superactivation to γ2 (L1 γ8 in γ2, 27 ± 6%, n = 10; Figure 4A and C and Table 1) but the reverse swap could not reduce superactivation to the level of γ2 (L1 γ2 in γ8, 16 ± 1%, n = 16; Figure 4B and C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Residual levels of superactivation of 6 ± 2 and 16 ± 3% (for γ2 and γ8, respectively, n = 6) were still present in the absence of L1.
source: The reason for this asymmetry became clear when we recorded complexes from which we removed L1 altogether from each TARP. Residual levels of superactivation of 6 ± 2 and 16 ± 3% (for γ2 and γ8, respectively, n = 6; Table 1) were still present in the absence of L1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Table 1.

claim: Although loop 1 can contribute to superactivation, and increase it over baseline levels, it is not the only element of TARPs driving this effect.
source: Therefore, although loop 1 can contribute to superactivation, and increase it over baseline levels, it is not the only element of TARPs driving this effect.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing residual superactivation in the absence of L1.

claim: Neutralizing L2 in γ2 (γ2 L2_GS) substantially reduced superactivation (1.3 ± 0.6%, n = 8).
source: Given the residual superactivation that we saw in the absence of loop 1, we reasoned that loop 2 could play a role in receptor superactivation (Figure 5). We measured responses to 10 mM glutamate for the L2_GS mutants of γ2 and γ8 and found substantially reduced superactivation (1.3 ± 0.6 and 12 ± 2%, n = 8 and 4, respectively; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Neutralizing L2 in γ8 (γ8 L2_GS) substantially reduced superactivation (12 ± 2%, n = 4).
source: Given the residual superactivation that we saw in the absence of loop 1, we reasoned that loop 2 could play a role in receptor superactivation (Figure 5). We measured responses to 10 mM glutamate for the L2_GS mutants of γ2 and γ8 and found substantially reduced superactivation (1.3 ± 0.6 and 12 ± 2%, n = 8 and 4, respectively; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The loop 1 from γ2 in the L2_GS mutant of γ8 had almost negligible superactivation, reduced by ~15 fold from wild-type γ8, to about 1 ± 0.7% (n = 6).
source: Even more strikingly, the same TARP mutants with loop 1 swapped had a further reduced effect. The loop 1 from γ2 in the L2_GS mutant of γ8 had almost negligible superactivation, reduced by ~15 fold from wild-type γ8, to about 1 ± 0.7% (n = 6; Figure 5B and C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The L1 γ2 in γ8 L2_GS mutant is classed as a kinetic null of γ8.
source: Taking into account the lack of steady-state current, fast desensitization and similar deactivation kinetics to wild-type GluA2 alone that we observed in patches containing complexes of GluA2 with the L1 γ2 in γ8 L2_GS mutant, we classed this chimera as a kinetic null of γ8.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and inference about the functional properties of the mutant.

claim: γ2 ΔL1 L2_GS associated normally into the receptor complex but was highly deficient in modulating gating of GluA2.
source: We reasoned that a γ2 chimera lacking L1 and with a GS-linker replacing L2 should associate normally with GluA2 but might have no kinetic effect at all on the receptor complexes. Indeed, γ2 ΔL1 L2_GS associated normally into the receptor complex (as assessed by relief of polyamine block, Figure 6A and B) but this mutant γ2 was highly deficient in modulating gating of GluA2.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 6.

claim: Superactivation and the increase in steady state current were absent in γ2 ΔL1 L2_GS complexes (superactivation = 0%; Iss = 2 ± 1%, n = 4 and 5, respectively).
source: Superactivation, and the increase in steady state current were absent in these complexes (superactivation = 0%; Iss = 2 ± 1%, n = 4 and 5, respectively; Figure 6C and D and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: The deletion of L1 from γ8 on the L2-GS background retained a larger steady state current than the chimera that included the L1 segment of γ2 (Iss = 5 ± 1% and 10 ± 5%, n = 6 and 5, for L1 γ2 in γ8 L2_GS and γ8 ΔL1 L2_GS, respectively).
source: Somewhat surprisingly, the deletion of L1 from γ8 on the L2-GS background retained a larger steady state current than the chimera that included the L1 segment of γ2 (Iss = 5 ± 1% and 10 ± 5%, n = 6 and 5, for L1 γ2 in γ8 L2_GS and γ8 ΔL1 L2_GS, respectively; Figures 5B and C and 6E and F and Table 1) and a small superactivation (3 ± 1%, n = 4; Figure 6A and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figures 5, 6 and Table 1.

claim: L2 is well placed to interact with the S1-M1 linker and the S2-M4 linker in the AMPA receptor.
source: Substitutions at L2 of γ2 and γ8 had profound effects on gating of TARP complexes and are well placed to interact with gating machinery (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). Particularly, we expected from our structural models and other available structural data (Twomey et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016) that L2 should interact with the S1-M1 linker and the S2-M4 linker in the AMPA receptor.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling and inference from published structures.

claim: Previous work has shown the importance of the S1-M1 and S2-M4 linkers in glutamate receptor gating.
source: Previous work has shown the importance of these linkers in glutamate receptor gating (Balannik et al., 2005; Schmid et al., 2007; Talukder et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balannik et al., 2005, Schmid et al., 2007, and Talukder et al., 2010.

claim: The L2 sequence has an alternating charge motif that is mirrored in two parts of the GluA2 linkers 508QKS510 and 781KEK783.
source: The L2 sequence has an alternating charge motif (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that is mirrored in two parts of the GluA2 linkers 508QKS510 and 781KEK783.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Replacement of 508QKS510 to GAG in the S1-M1 linker (GluA2 508GAG510) produced a GluA2 receptor with normal kinetics that associated normally with γ2 and γ8.
source: Replacement of 508QKS510 (conserved among AMPA receptor subunits) to GAG in the S1-M1 linker (GluA2 508GAG510, Figure 7A) produced a GluA2 receptor with normal kinetics and that associated normally with γ2 and γ8 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In complexes with WT γ2, the GluA2 508GAG510 mutant abolished superactivation and reduced the steady state current (0% and 10 ± 5%, n = 3 and 4, for superactivation and Iss, respectively).
source: Strikingly, in complexes with WT γ2, this mutant phenocopied the neutralizing truncation of L2 in TARPs well (see Figure 3), abolishing superactivation and reducing the steady state current (0% and 10 ± 5%, n = 3 and 4, for superactivation and Iss, respectively; Figure 7C–E and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: A point mutant K509A had normal gating and was more strongly modulated by γ2.
source: In contrast, a point mutant K509A, also with normal gating (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), was more strongly modulated by γ2, providing further indication that a second site was potentially involved (Figure 7E and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The triple mutation replacing 781KEK783 to GSG (GluA2 781GSG783) had normal kinetics in the absence of γ2 but exhibited a reduced steady state current and negligible superactivation (10 ± 1% and 2 ± 0.5%, n = 9 and 8, for Iss and superactivation respectively).
source: To test the importance of the alternating charges in the S2-M4 linker, we made another triple mutation replacing 781KEK783 (KDK in GluA1, A3, A4) to GSG (GluA2 781GSG783, Figure 7B). This mutant again had normal kinetics in the absence of γ2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but also exhibited a reduced steady state current and negligible superactivation (10 ± 1% and 2 ± 0.5%, n = 9 and 8, for Iss and superactivation respectively; Figure 7C–E and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The combination of the two triple mutants (GluA2 GAG/GSG) abolished the entire modulatory effect of γ2 on the AMPA receptor, reducing superactivation and the instantaneous steady-state current to the same level as GluA2 in the absence of TARP (0% and 5 ± 1%, n = 4 and 8, for superactivation and Iss, respectively).
source: Importantly, the combination of these two triple mutants, abolished the entire modulatory effect of γ2 on the AMPA receptor, reducing superactivation and the instantaneous steady-state current to the same level as GluA2 in the absence of TARP (0% and 5 ± 1%, n = 4 and 8, for superactivation and Iss, respectively; Figure 7C–E and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The GluA2 GAG/GSG mutant receptor retained ostensibly normal gating and association to TARPs, despite the absence of gating modulation.
source: This mutant receptor retained ostensibly normal gating and association to TARPs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), despite the absence of gating modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from electrophysiology recordings presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The long loop of γ8 L1 is still able to modulate complexes at extracellular sites with the receptor linker sites disrupted.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the long loop of γ8 L1 is still able to modulate complexes at extracellular sites with the receptor linker sites disrupted, supporting the idea that the linkers do not function primarily to transduce distant TARP modulation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing that γ8 can still modulate the double linker mutant.

claim: The LBD-TMD linkers are the primary modulatory site for both γ8 and γ2.
source: Rather, the LBD-TMD linkers are the primary modulatory site for both γ8 and γ2.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that mutations in the linkers abolish modulation.

claim: γ2 has a short L1 loop, and cannot modulate receptors if the L2 interaction is absent.
source: The latter has a short L1 loop, and cannot modulate receptors if the L2 interaction is absent.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that γ2 L2_GS has no modulatory effect.

claim: γ8 combines the longer L1 and the L2 site to modulate receptor properties more effectively, in a compound fashion.
source: However, γ8 combines the longer L1 and the L2 site to modulate receptor properties more effectively, in a compound fashion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that γ8 modulation requires both L1 and L2.

claim: Extracellular sites account for all the modification of AMPA receptor gating by TARPs.
source: The results we present here offer several new insights into TARP function. First of all, extracellular sites account for all the modification of AMPA receptor gating by TARPs.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The extracellular sites do not have any appreciable role in determining assembly of TARP-AMPA receptor complexes.
source: Secondly, these same sites do not have any appreciable role in determining assembly of TARP-AMPA receptor complexes.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data showing that mutants with altered extracellular loops still assemble normally.

claim: Interactions between transmembrane segments and intracellular regions are responsible for assembly and modulation of polyamine block.
source: Interactions between transmembrane segments and intracellular regions are responsible for assembly and modulation of polyamine block.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and established knowledge in the field.

claim: State-dependent gating modification results from transient interactions on a timescale far faster than receptor assembly.
source: We speculate that this division of roles arises because state-dependent gating modification results from transient interactions on a timescale far faster than receptor assembly.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanistic basis of the observed division of roles.

claim: The linkers to the transmembrane domain are key sites for modulation of AMPA receptor gating by auxiliary proteins.
source: Thirdly, we show that the linkers to the transmembrane domain are key sites for modulation of AMPA receptor gating by auxiliary proteins, and provide insights into the molecular basis of this interaction.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The identified sites in the LBD-TMD linkers are highly conserved among all AMPA receptor subunits but not present in the related NMDA and kainate receptors.
source: The identified sites in the LBD-TMD linkers are highly conserved among all AMPA receptor subunits but not present in the related NMDA and kainate receptors, which are not modulated by TARPs.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge about TARP modulation specificity.

claim: Previous work suggested ATD interactions and prominent roles for the LBD in modulation of AMPARs by TARPs.
source: Previous work suggested ATD interactions and prominent roles for the LBD in modulation of AMPARs by TARPs, but the interactions we demonstrate here are much more proximal to the channel gate (Cais et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cais et al., 2014.

claim: The interactions demonstrated in this study are much more proximal to the channel gate than previously suggested ATD and LBD interactions.
source: Previous work suggested ATD interactions and prominent roles for the LBD in modulation of AMPARs by TARPs, but the interactions we demonstrate here are much more proximal to the channel gate (Cais et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing that the linker regions are the key modulatory sites.

claim: The elimination of modulation by nullifying L2 of γ2, or by mutating residues in the LBD-TMD linkers of GluA2, strongly implicates this site as a pivotal interaction underlying modulation.
source: We could show a very close functional confluence between modifying the receptor itself and modifying each TARP, at an interaction site predicted from structural modeling. The elimination of modulation by nullifying L2 of γ2, or by mutating residues in the LBD-TMD linkers of GluA2, strongly implicates this site as a pivotal interaction underlying modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing that mutations in either L2 or the linkers abolish modulation.

claim: Putative electrostatic interactions posited from structural studies require a large conformational change (between 13 Å and 25 Å depending on the TARP's position in the complex).
source: Putative electrostatic interactions posited from structural studies require a large conformational change (between 13 Å and 25 Å depending on the TARP's position in the complex; measured between C-alpha atoms from GluA2 K699 and γ2 D92 in cryo-EM complexes 5kbu and 5kk2, respectively) (Twomey et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of published cryo-EM structures.

claim: The L2-linker interactions are secondary to interactions involving the negative patch.
source: A key point here is that these interactions are secondary to those involving L2 at the AMPAR linkers.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that L2 interactions are dominant for modulation.

claim: The L2-linker interactions should occur readily for each auxiliary protein subunit, allowing a maximal 4:4 stoichiometry with minimal conformational change for γ2.
source: These interactions should occur readily for each auxiliary protein subunit, allowing a maximal 4:4 stoichiometry with minimal conformational change for γ2 (Figure 8A) (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural modeling and published data, with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: For γ8, the stoichiometry of the L2-linker interaction would vary with the number of associated TARPs, but will not be limited by position of the TARP within the complex.
source: For other auxiliary proteins, for example γ8, the stoichiometry of the L2-linker interaction would vary with the number of associated TARPs, but will not be limited by position of the TARP within the complex (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural modeling, with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Neutralization of the major part of the acidic patch strongly enhanced modulation of gating by γ2, ruling out that negative charges here have a dominant role in modulation.
source: Finally, neutralization of the major part of the acidic patch strongly enhanced modulation of gating by γ2, ruling out that negative charges here have a dominant role in modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The slow increase in glutamate efficacy (superactivation) is specified by the combination of L1 and L2.
source: Our results allow us to construct a tentative model for the distinct forms of modulation that TARPs produce (Figure 8C). The slow increase in glutamate efficacy, which we term superactivation, is specified by the combination of L1 and L2, whereas the basal increase in steady state current arises from L2 alone.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The basal increase in steady state current arises from L2 alone.
source: Our results allow us to construct a tentative model for the distinct forms of modulation that TARPs produce (Figure 8C). The slow increase in glutamate efficacy, which we term superactivation, is specified by the combination of L1 and L2, whereas the basal increase in steady state current arises from L2 alone.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The concerted involvement of multiple loops suggests multiple conformational states are required to describe the interaction, most notably in the case of γ8.
source: The concerted involvement of multiple loops suggests multiple conformational states are required to describe the interaction, most notably in the case of γ8.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that both L1 and L2 contribute to modulation.

claim: The greater conformational space that can be explored by loop 1, and its strong connection to superactivation, indicate that these conformational changes could relate to the slow transitions represented in the model of superactivation.
source: The greater conformational space that can be explored by loop 1, and its strong connection to superactivation, indicate that these conformational changes could relate to the slow transitions represented in the model of superactivation (Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the experimental data and a citation to Carbone and Plested, 2016.

claim: Conformational changes of the linker region of the AMPA receptor upon opening will naturally lead to a state-dependent interaction with L2 of γ2 or γ8, because of the direct proximity.
source: In contrast, conformational changes of the linker region of the AMPA receptor upon opening will naturally lead to a state-dependent interaction with L2 of γ2 or γ8, because of the direct proximity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the structural models and experimental data.

claim: An intact L2 segment is required for the strong superactivation induced by γ8, but is not required at all for slow desensitization behavior that the long L1 loop of γ8 can produce.
source: A further level of complexity is that an intact L2 segment is required for the strong superactivation induced by γ8, but is not required at all for slow desensitization behavior that the long L1 loop of γ8 can produce.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing differential effects of L1 and L2 mutations.

claim: L1 adopts multiple conformations to stabilize separate functional states of the receptor, and some functional signatures require a concerted action of both loops.
source: Because in these experiments, slow desensitization occurs when occupancy of superactive states is low, we can quite reasonably assume that L1 adopts multiple conformations to stabilize separate functional states of the receptor, and that some functional signatures require a concerted action of both loops.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that L1 and L2 have distinct and combined effects.

claim: Additional stabilization of desensitized states by the variable loop 1 is also likely.
source: Additional stabilization of desensitized states by the variable loop 1 is also likely (Twomey et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by a citation to Twomey et al., 2017a.

claim: This work has produced mutant TARPs and AMPA receptors that both lack modulatory properties, and also those that have greatly enhanced modulation.
source: This work has produced mutant TARPs and AMPA receptors that both lack modulatory properties, and also those that have greatly enhanced modulation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mutants produced should be useful tools for investigating TARP action in synapses.
source: Both these signatures of activity should be useful tools for investigating TARP action in synapses, including understanding the relative importance of assembly into complexes for anchoring (Opazo et al., 2010) as opposed to kinetic modulation, for clarifying the consequences of TARP modulation for short term plasticity (Devi et al., 2016), and for better identifying TARPs in ternary complexes with other auxiliary subunits (Khodosevich et al., 2014; Herring et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculation about the potential applications of the findings, with citations to relevant work.

claim: An open AMPAR structure in complex with TARP γ2 was released while this manuscript was being revised.
source: Whilst this manuscript was being revised, an open AMPAR structure in complex with TARP γ2 was released (Twomey et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is a statement of fact about a published structure, supported by a citation to Twomey et al., 2017b.

claim: The loops analyzed in this study are not resolved in the open AMPAR structure, but this structure places the unstructured L2 in close apposition with the linker regions of the AMPAR, consistent with the idea of state-dependent L2 interactions and modulation.
source: The loops that we analyze here are not resolved, but this structure (like previous closed state structures) places the unstructured L2 in close apposition with the linker regions of the AMPAR, consistent with our idea of state-dependent L2 interactions and modulation.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of a published structure and comparison with the findings of this study.

claim: GluA2 flip receptors, unedited at the pore site (Q-containing) were used in this study.
source: We used GluA2 flip receptors, unedited at the pore site (Q-containing) in the pRK vector also expressing eGFP following an internal ribosomal entry site (IRES) sequence.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental materials used in the study.

claim: Mouse γ2 was expressed from an IRES-dsRed construct.
source: Mouse γ2 was the kind gift of Susumu Tomita and was expressed from an IRES-dsRed construct as previously described (Carbone and Plested, 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental materials used in the study, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Mouse γ8 was expressed from an IRES-dsRed construct.
source: Mouse γ8 (the kind gift of Roger Nicoll) was expressed the same way.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental materials used in the study.

claim: Point mutations and chimeras were created by overlap PCR and confirmed by double-stranded sequencing.
source: Point mutations and chimeras were created by overlap PCR and confirmed by double-stranded sequencing.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Residues in GluA2 were numbered based on the assumption that the signal peptide is 21 residues.
source: Residues in GluA2 were numbered based on the assumption that the signal peptide is 21 residues.
evidence: The claim describes the numbering convention used in the study.

claim: Wild type or mutant GluA2 and TARP constructs were co-transfected with PEI in HEK 293 cells.
source: Wild type or mutant GluA2 and TARP constructs were co-transfected with PEI in HEK 293 cells (obtained from the Leibniz-Institut DSMZ - Deutsche Sammlung von Mikroorganismen und Zellkulturen GmbH; DSMZ no.: ACC 305).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The ratios of co-transfection were 1:2 for GluA2-γ2 and 1:5 for GluA2-γ8.
source: The ratios of co-transfection were 1:2 for GluA2-γ2 and 1:5 for GluA2-γ8, up to 2 μg total DNA per 35 mm dish.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Cells were supplemented with 40 μM NBQX to reduce TARP-induced cytotoxicity.
source: Cells were supplemented with 40 μM NBQX to reduce TARP-induced cytotoxicity.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Recordings were performed 24–48 hr after transfection.
source: Recordings were performed 24–48 hr after transfection.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: 10 mM glutamate was applied to outside-out patches with a piezo-driven fast perfusion system.
source: 10 mM glutamate was applied to outside-out patches with a piezo-driven fast perfusion system (PI, Germany).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Patches were voltage-clamped at a holding potential of +50 mV to isolate currents exclusively mediated by AMPAR-TARP complexes.
source: In order to isolate currents exclusively mediated by AMPAR-TARP complexes, patches were voltage-clamped at a holding potential of +50 mV.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Typical 10–90% solution exchange times were faster than 300 µs.
source: Typical 10–90% solution exchange times were faster than 300 µs, as measured from junction potentials at the open tip of the patch pipette.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods and quality control used in the study.

claim: Desensitization rate and steady-state current were obtained by fitting the traces with a sum of two, and when necessary three, exponentials.
source: To measure receptor desensitization we applied 10 mM glutamate for 500 ms. Desensitization rate and steady-state current were then obtained by fitting the traces with a sum of two, and when necessary three, exponentials.
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis methods used in the study.

claim: Superactivation was measured during a 7 s application of glutamate and was defined as the excess steady-state amplitude following the desensitization trough, normalized to the peak current.
source: Superactivation was measured during a 7 s application of glutamate and was defined as the excess steady-state amplitude following the desensitization trough, normalized to the peak current.
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis methods used in the study.

claim: The rectification index (RI) was calculated as the ratio between the current amplitude recorded at +60 mV and that recorded at −60 mV.
source: The rectification index (RI) was calculated as the ratio between the current amplitude recorded at +60 mV and that recorded at −60 mV.
evidence: The claim describes the data analysis methods used in the study.

claim: At least 5–6 patches from at least three different transfections were recorded for each condition.
source: To account for possible variability in the response and expression of the complexes, we tried to record at least 5–6 patches from at least three different transfections for each condition.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and sample size used in the study.

claim: Structural models of TARP γ2 and γ8 were generated based on the crystal structure of claudin15 using the SWISS-MODEL and ProtMod server.
source: Initial γ2 and γ8 models were generated based on the crystal structure of claudin15 (PDB code: 4P79) using the SWISS-MODEL (Arnold et al., 2006) and ProtMod server (part of the FFAS server, [Jaroszewski et al., 2011]).
evidence: The claim describes the structural modeling methods used in the study, with citations to the tools used.

claim: COOT was used to superpose the two generated models and to build the final model with an intact helix 3 and plausible extracellular loops 1 and 2.
source: Thus, we used COOT (version 0.8.7) to superpose the two generated models and to build the final model with an intact helix 3 and plausible extracellular loops 1 and 2.
evidence: The claim describes the structural modeling methods used in the study.

claim: The TARP models were validated using MolProbity.
source: The TARP models were validated using MolProbity (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim describes the structural modeling methods used in the study, with a citation to the tool used.

claim: Weak coupling was detected for the steady-state current, but coupling of approximately 4.5 kJ/Mol was detected for superactivation.
source: With the caveat that we can at best measure a level of current of about 1% of the peak current, limiting the resolution of the reduction in current upon mutation, we could detect only weak coupling for the steady-state current, but coupling of approximately 4.5 kJ/Mol in the case of superactivation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on thermodynamic cycle analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.
